content: When managing bacterial meningitis in settings where there is no significant resistance to chloramphenicol and beta-lactam antibiotics, national guidelines should be followed. Alternatively, two treatment regimens can be used: (1) chloramphenicol at 25 mg/kg administered intramuscularly (IM) or intravenously (IV) every 6 hours, combined with ampicillin at 50 mg/kg IM or IV every 6 hours; or (2) chloramphenicol at the same dose and frequency, combined with benzyl penicillin at 60 mg/kg (100,000 units/kg) IM or IV every 6 hours. This recommendation is conditional and based on moderate-quality evidence. For measles, there are currently no GRC-approved recommendations. Updated guidance is in progress, but in the meantime, the 2004 guidelines for treating measles in children may be used. In cases of septicemia, no GRC-approved recommendations exist, and guidance is being updated. Ciprofloxacin, gatifloxacin, ofloxacin, or perfloxacin can be used as first-line treatments for 7–10 days. Ciprofloxacin is recommended at 15 mg/kg per dose orally twice daily for 7–10 days. If treatment response is poor, consider drug-resistant typhoid and treat with second-line antibiotics such as third-generation cephalosporins or azithromycin. Options include ceftriaxone (IV) at 80 mg/kg per day for 5–7 days or azithromycin at 20 mg/kg per day for 5–7 days. Where local data on antibiotic resistance among Salmonella isolates is available, national guidelines should be followed. These are strong recommendations based on moderate-quality evidence. Children with MUAC less than 115 mm or any degree of bilateral edema should be referred immediately for full assessment at a treatment center. Health workers in primary care facilities and hospitals should assess MUAC, weight-for-height/length, and bilateral edema. Children meeting these criteria should be admitted to a SAM management program. These are strong recommendations based on low-quality evidence. Children with SAM should undergo a full clinical examination to determine the presence of medical complications. Those who are clinically well, alert, and have an appetite can be treated as outpatients. Children with medical complications, severe edema, poor appetite, or danger signs (e.g., inability to drink, convulsions, lethargy) should be treated as inpatients. Children admitted to hospitals for SAM can be transferred to outpatient care once medical complications, including edema, are resolving, and they are clinically well and alert with a good appetite. Discharge from treatment should occur only when weight-for-height/length is ≥ -2 Z-scores or MUAC is ≥ 125 mm, with no edema for at least 2 weeks. These are strong recommendations based on low-quality evidence. Children with SAM who are managed as outpatients should receive a course of oral antibiotics, such as amoxicillin or another broad-spectrum antibiotic. However, undernourished children without SAM should not routinely receive antibiotics unless they show signs of clinical infection. Children with SAM should receive the recommended daily intake of vitamin A through therapeutic foods or a multi-micronutrient formula. High-dose vitamin A supplementation is not required if the therapeutic foods already meet WHO specifications. These are strong recommendations based on low-quality evidence. For therapeutic feeding, children with SAM and diarrhea can be given ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) in the same way as those without diarrhea. In inpatient settings, children transitioning from stabilization to rehabilitation should move from F-75 to RUTF over 2–3 days, as tolerated. Children admitted with complicated SAM and achieving rapid weight gain on F-100 should transition to RUTF before being transferred to outpatient care. These are strong recommendations based on very low-quality evidence. For fluid management in children with SAM, rehydration should be done slowly using oral or nasogastric rehydration solutions (ORS) specifically designed for malnourished children. Standard WHO low-osmolarity ORS should not be used. Children with SAM and signs of shock or severe dehydration who cannot be rehydrated orally should receive IV fluids, such as half-strength Darrow’s solution with 5% dextrose or Ringer’s lactate with 5% dextrose. These are strong or conditional recommendations based on low-quality evidence. HIV-infected children with SAM should start antiretroviral therapy (ART) as soon as possible after stabilization of metabolic complications and sepsis. ART regimens and doses should be the same as for HIV-infected children without SAM. Close monitoring is required during the first 6–8 weeks of ART initiation to identify complications. HIV-infected children with SAM should receive the same therapeutic feeding approaches as HIV-uninfected children with SAM. These are strong recommendations based on very low-quality evidence. Infants under 6 months of age with SAM and complicating factors (e.g., medical complications, recent weight loss, ineffective feeding, or pitting edema) should be admitted for inpatient care. Feeding approaches should prioritize establishing or re-establishing effective exclusive breastfeeding. If breastfeeding is not possible, supplementary feeding with expressed breast milk, infant formula, or F-75 may be used. Undiluted F-100 should not be given due to the risk of hypernatremia. Infants can be transferred to outpatient care when medical complications are resolved, they are clinically well, and they have adequate weight gain. Discharge from care should occur when they are feeding well and have achieved adequate weight gain. These are strong recommendations based on very low-quality evidence. For moderate acute malnutrition (MAM), management should include breastfeeding promotion, nutrition counseling, and addressing underlying causes of malnutrition, such as food insecurity. Nutrient-dense foods should be provided to meet the extra needs for weight and height gain. Proposed nutrient compositions for supplementary foods are available for reference. For HIV diagnosis in infants and children, nucleic acid testing (NAT) at birth can be considered for early infant diagnosis (EID). For children older than 18 months, RDTs can diagnose HIV following national testing strategies. Provider-initiated HIV testing and counseling should be routinely offered to infants and children with unknown HIV status in generalized epidemic settings, particularly in inpatient and malnutrition clinics. These are strong or conditional recommendations based on low-quality evidence. Adolescents living with HIV should receive HIV testing and counseling with linkages to prevention, treatment, and care. Community-based approaches and training of healthcare workers can improve treatment adherence and retention in care. These are strong recommendations based on low-quality evidence. These include case management, patient tracing, peer support, and quality improvement approaches. CD4 cell count testing at the point of care can help prioritize patients for urgent ART initiation. Electronic communication can reduce delays in acting on test results. These are conditional recommendations based on low-quality evidence.
